the ribosome is a very useful matrix to purify translation factors.

(i) the ribosome can be used as an 'immobilized' affinity matrix to selectively eluted the non-ribosom proteins required for the translation; and (ii) a scheme for the purification, in homogeneous form of each of these factors is described.

the study of the mechanisms of translation in vitro.
the study of the mechanism of translation and the role of its components.

the ribosome can be used as an 'immobilized' affinity matrix to selectively elicit the non-ribosomally synthesized proteins required to translate an mRNA in vitro.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ribosome is a convenient matrix for the purification of all the nonribosomal proteins required in the translation of native mRNAs in vitro.
we can now reconstruct translation in vitro with a set of purified components.

, using this method, we have isolated, in homogeneous form: (i) 20S ribosomal subunit, (ii) 50S ribosomal subunits (iii) 30S ribosomal sub-units, (iv) 70S ribosomes, (v) initiation factors, (vi) elongation factors, (vii) EF-P, (viii) W proteins and (ix) all the aminoacyl-tRNAsynthetases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to use the ribosome as an 'affinit' matrix' to selectively elute non-ribosomal translation factors.

it is not necessary to use a complicated purification scheme to purify the proteins required to translate an mRNA in vitro, and the ribosomal subunits themselves can be used as 'affinity' matrices to elute the proteins bound to them.
